title: Approval of American Society of Mechanical Engineers Unconditioned Code Cases
summary:
Today’s Federal Register delivers three notable moves: disaster aid paperwork for livestock producers is officially cleared, the nuclear regulator is streamlining how plants can use vetted engineering alternatives, and aviation safety rules for certain Bombardier jets are being tightened.

First, the Department of Agriculture’s Farm Service Agency confirmed that the information it needs to process Emergency Livestock Relief payments for 2023–2024 floods and wildfires has been approved. That means payments can move forward using existing forms plus one new form, with approval running through late 2027. Producers hit by extreme weather stand to benefit from faster access to help. On the downside, the agency estimates a large overall time burden across applicants, and smaller or remote operations may find the process demanding, even with assistance options and disability accommodations in place.

Second, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a direct final rule that incorporates a new regulatory guide approving a set of American Society of Mechanical Engineers “code cases” without extra conditions. In plain terms, nuclear power plant applicants and licensees can use these pre-approved alternatives to certain engineering standards, which can save time and keep maintenance and testing aligned with current best practices. The commission says safety is maintained, there’s no significant environmental impact, and the material is being made reasonably available for public viewing. Plants and vendors gain flexibility and predictability. Critics may worry about relying more on industry-developed standards or about the complexity of tracking updates across multiple guides. If you have concerns, the agency is taking public comments until November 25, 2025; the rule takes effect January 26, 2026 unless significant adverse comments are received.

Finally, the Federal Aviation Administration adopted a new safety rule for Bombardier CL‑600 series aircraft. Operators must update their maintenance and inspection programs to include new or more restrictive limits. Passengers and crews benefit from stronger safety margins. Operators, however, will face added work to revise programs and may see higher maintenance costs or downtime to comply.

Overall, these actions aim to speed relief, modernize safety oversight, and keep critical infrastructure reliable, while shifting some paperwork and compliance costs to those affected.
